requirements.summary: useradd -m datauser succeeded, confirmed with id showing uid=1000(datauser).

requirements.requirement: datauser is limited to 100MB of storage under /srv/data, enforced by the filesystem itself
requirements.summary: A dedicated XFS loopback filesystem was created and mounted at /srv/data with the uquota/usrquota mount option, and an XFS user quota (bsoft=bhard=100m) was set for datauser via xfs_quota, which is kernel-level filesystem enforcement rather than application logic. Enforcement was directly demonstrated: a 150MB write as datauser was truncated at exactly 100MB with 'Disk quota exceeded', while a 10MB write succeeded and the quota report reflected correct usage.

requirements.requirement: Quota configuration is persistent (survives remount/reboot) so the limit remains enforced going forward
requirements.summary: fstab entry with loop,uquota options was added (backing up original fstab), and a full reboot was captured with a bounded disruption: pre-restart baseline (boot_id 34027437-..., quota usage 10M/100M, data present), a reboot acknowledgement, a changed post-restart boot_id (8e10fe6f-...), and post-restart verification showing /srv/data auto-remounted with usrquota, data intact, and the 100MB limit still enforced (a 150MB write again failed with 'Disk quota exceeded').

overall_summary: The task's material outcomes — creation of datauser, a 100MB quota on /srv/data enforced natively by the XFS filesystem, and persistence of that enforcement across a reboot — are all directly and coherently evidenced by command output (account creation, quota configuration, over-limit write failing exactly at 100MB, under-limit write succeeding, and full pre/post-reboot verification with a changed boot_id). Hygiene is good overall, with only a trivial leftover temp file as a minor blemish.
limitations: No independent confirmation was captured that the recovered post-reboot state used the exact same loop device/backing file rather than a fresh remount artifact, though the fstab persistence and matching quota report make this highly likely.
The /tmp/fstab.new leftover file was not explicitly cleaned up in the trace; it is low-risk but represents a minor untracked residue.

operational_hygiene.summary: Executor commands were tightly scoped to the task: install quota tooling, create user, build a dedicated loopback XFS filesystem (avoiding a risky in-place remount of the root filesystem, which is a sound design choice since root was 'noquota'), configure and verify the quota, and run the mandated restart protocol. The fstab edit was preceded by a backup (/etc/fstab.bak), and the reboot was a necessary, fully-recovered, bounded disruption used only to validate persistence. One small residue: /tmp/fstab.new (an intermediate scratch file used to build the new fstab) was left behind rather than cleaned up after cmd-093e98a56002491b, visible in the after_executor temporary-files snapshot. This is low-risk residue (a leftover text file, not a security or service issue) and does not affect functionality. No failed or conflicting services, no unnecessary or destructive mutations, and no weakened security controls were observed (listening-socket and failed-service snapshots are unchanged in substance across the restart, differing only by PID).
